title: So I Tried That Pineapple Tallow Balm Everyone's Talking About
body:
Okay look. I need to talk about this beef tallow stuff I’ve been putting on my face. The pineapple one. I know. It sounds insane. Beef fat? On your skin? In 2024? I thought the same thing. My brain went straight to candles or something. But my hands were a disaster this spring—like, cracking, red, the whole thing—and I’d tried everything from the drugstore. The $12 lotion, the $28 “healing” cream in the silver tube, you name it. Nothing stuck. My skin just drank it and asked for more. I was scrolling on my phone one night, it was like 11:30, and I fell into this whole internet hole about traditional tallow skincare. People were swearing by it. And not just any tallow, but whipped tallow balm, specifically from grass-fed cows. Made in France, apparently. The algorithm had me. I was skeptical, obviously. But my knuckles were so bad I’d catch them on my sweater. So I figured, what’s the worst that could happen? I ordered the pineapple-scented one from this little Etsy shop because, I don’t know, it sounded less intimidating. “Tropical escape,” it said. Sounded better than “plain beef fat.” A week later, this little jar shows up.

## How Beef Tallow for Skin Became a Thing Again (According to My Internet Dive)

So here’s the weird history lesson I got. Using tallow on skin isn’t new. It’s like, ancient. My grandma, if I think about it, probably knew about it. She had all those old-school remedies—lard for cooking, sure, but also for chapped hands in winter. I never connected the dots until I started reading. For centuries, before all the chemical labs and fancy factories, people used what they had. Animal fats were a big part of that. They’d render down the suet from beef—that’s the fat around the kidneys—clean it up, and use it as a base for salves and balms. It fell out of fashion for obvious reasons. “Putting beef fat on your face” doesn’t sound great in a glossy magazine ad next to something with hyaluronic acid and a French name. It got labeled as gross, old-fashioned, poor people’s stuff. But the thing is, biologically, it makes a stupid amount of sense. Our skin’s natural oil, sebum? It has a similar fatty acid profile to tallow. Like, really similar. So the idea is that your skin recognizes it. It doesn’t just sit on top like a greasy film from some lotions; it actually gets absorbed because it’s compatible. It’s a moisturizer that speaks your skin’s language. The whole “natural skincare comeback” isn’t just about plants. It’s about stuff that actually works, even if it seems weird at first. This is that. It’s a traditional tallow skincare thing making a comeback because people are tired of buying expensive bottles of water and chemicals that don’t do anything.

## What This Pineapple Tallow Balm Actually Does (On My Skin, Anyway)

The jar is small. Cute, though. When I opened it, I braced myself. I was expecting a meat locker smell or something truly bizarre. It didn’t smell like beef. At all. It smelled… fruity. Sweet. Like pineapple, yeah, but not a fake candy pineapple. More like if you walked past a smoothie shop on a hot day. Cheerful. Vacation feeling, for sure. The texture threw me. I poked it. It was whipped, so it’s super light and airy, not a hard waxy chunk. It melts the second it touches your skin warmth. I put a tiny bit on the back of my hand. It vanished. No greasy residue. No shiny film. My skin just… ate it. And it felt soft. Not “soft to the touch” in a commercial way, but normal-soft. Like my skin used to feel before winter wrecked it. That was the first test. I started using it on my cracking knuckles and cuticles. Within a couple days, the cracks started to heal. Not just get a little better, but actually seal up. I was shocked. So I got brave. My face has these dry patches on the cheeks, especially in spring with the weird weather—warm one day, windy the next. I started using a pea-sized amount at night. Just rubbed it between my palms and patted it on. Same thing. It absorbed. Didn’t break me out. Didn’t feel heavy. I woke up and my skin wasn’t tight. It just felt… calm. I don’t know how else to say it. It’s not a miracle. It’s just a really good moisturizer. It mimics sebum, so it gives your skin what it might be missing without clogging the works. For dry skin, chapped lips, rough hands? It’s a game-changer. I used it on my elbows too. They’re notoriously rough. They’re smoother now. It’s wild.

## My Skin After a Few Weeks & Would I Buy It Again

I’ve been using it for about a month now. Maybe six weeks. I’m not a skincare influencer. I don’t have “before and after” photos. But I can tell you what happened. My hands are normal. That’s the biggest thing. I don’t think about them anymore. I’m not hiding them in my pockets. The jar sits on my bedside table next to my water glass and a pile of old receipts. I use it every night. Sometimes in the morning if I’m feeling dry. My sister was over last week and she picked it up, smelled it, and said “what’s this?” I told her. She made a face. Then she tried it. She stole a little scoop for her own hands. Texted me two days later asking for the link. That’s the real test, right? I’m on my second jar now. The first one lasted a surprisingly long time because you need so little. I got the new one from the same Etsy shop—Mt Heritage, I think it’s called. The whole process felt personal, not like ordering from a giant corporation. So yeah, I’d buy it again. I already did. It’s become one of those things I just have. Like my favorite brand of socks or the specific pen I like. It works. It’s simple. And after learning about the beef tallow history, it feels kind of cool to be using something so straightforward. No fifteen-step routine. No waiting for it to sink in. Just… balm. That happens to be made from tallow. And smells like pineapple.

## Quick Questions I Get Asked

**Is beef tallow good for your face?**
Yeah, it can be. It sounds wrong, I know. But because it’s so similar to our skin’s own oils, it absorbs really well. It doesn’t just sit there. It’s like giving your skin something it already understands how to use. My dry patches loved it.

**Does tallow balm clog pores?**
Not in my experience. And from what I read, because it’s so compatible with our skin, it’s actually less likely to clog pores than some mineral oil or silicone-based products. It just melts in. If you have super oily skin already, maybe just use a tiny bit. But for normal to dry skin, it’s been fine.

**What does the pineapple tallow balm smell like?**
It smells like pineapple. But a nice one. Not a cheap air freshener or candy. It’s sweet and fruity and just… pleasant. It doesn’t smell like cooking fat at all. The scent is cheerful. Makes the whole experience feel less clinical.

Anyway. If your skin is being difficult, or you’re just curious about this whole traditional tallow skincare thing, it might be worth a shot. I didn’t expect much. But honestly? It just works. My skin’s happy. I’m happy. That’s all I wanted.
